title: “Who had been carried away from Jerusalem … with Jeconiah” — Mordecai, or his forefather Kish?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The KJV names Mordecai “the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish” and goes on, “Who had been carried away from Jerusalem” with king Jeconiah. The verse does not say whether “who” is Mordecai or the last man named, Kish. The answer decides whether Mordecai himself came from Jerusalem, and so how long before the king’s seventh and twelfth years that carrying away lay.
text: KJV Esther 2:5: “Now in Shushan the palace there was a certain Jew, whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite;” KJV Esther 2:6: “Who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity which had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away.” KJV 2 Kings 24:15: “And he carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon” KJV Jeremiah 24:1: “after that Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon had carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah” KJV Esther 2:16: “in the seventh year of his reign” KJV Esther 3:7: “in the twelfth year of king Ahasuerus” Hebrew (WLC) 2:5: וּשְׁמֹ֣ו מָרְדֳּכַ֗י בֶּ֣ן יָאִ֧יר בֶּן־שִׁמְעִ֛י בֶּן־קִ֖ישׁ אִ֥ישׁ יְמִינִֽי [and his name Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjamite]; 2:6: אֲשֶׁ֤ר הָגְלָה֙ מִיר֣וּשָׁלַ֔יִם עִם־הַגֹּלָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָגְלְתָ֔ה עִ֖ם יְכָנְיָ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֑ה [who was carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity that was carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2:6: ὃς ἦν αἰχμάλωτος ἐξ Ἱερουσαλὴμ, ἣν ᾐχμαλώτευσε Ναβουχοδονόσορ βασιλεὺς Βαβυλῶνος. [who was a captive from Jerusalem, which Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon took captive]. In a passage the KJV does not have, the verse labelled 1:1c says of Mardochaeus: Ἦν δὲ ἐκ τῆς αἰχμαλωσίας, ἦς ᾐχμαλώτευσε Ναβουχοδονόσορ βασιλεὺς Βαβυλῶνος ἐξ Ἰερουσαλὴμ, μετὰ Ἰεχονίου τοῦ βασιλέως τῆς Ἰουδαίας. [and he was of the captivity which Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon took captive from Jerusalem, with Jechonias the king of Judaea]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/2/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG02.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG01.htm.
reasoning: The clause opens with a relative word that follows three forefathers’ names. Read of Mordecai, it makes him a man who was himself taken from Jerusalem in Jeconiah’s day and who is still active in the twelfth year of Ahasuerus. Read of Kish, it dates the family’s removal and says nothing of Mordecai’s age. The verses quoted do not say how many years lie between Jeconiah’s captivity and the reign of Ahasuerus, so the weight of the question depends on which king is meant as well.
scope: Readings, none stated in the two KJV verses: that “who” is Mordecai; that “who” is Kish, the nearest name; or that it speaks of the family as a whole. The Hebrew relative word and the Greek of 2:6 leave the same choice open. The Greek’s added verse 1:1c does state one reading, that Mordecai himself was of that captivity; the KJV and the Hebrew edition have no such verse. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV finds “Jeconiah” at 1 Chronicles 3:16 and 3:17, Esther 2:6 and Jeremiah 24:1, 27:20, 28:4 and 29:2; none of those verses names Mordecai or Kish. That is a word search, not a reading of every passage about the captivity. Which king Ahasuerus is has been asked in another record and is not settled here. This is not presented as a contradiction. title: “But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence” — why not?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The king commands that all bow to Haman, and Mordecai does not. He is asked why and no answer of his is reported; the passage says only that “he had told them that he was a Jew”. Haman’s plan to destroy all the Jews follows from this refusal, and the KJV does not state its reason.
text: KJV Esther 3:2: “And all the king's servants, that were in the king's gate, bowed, and reverenced Haman: for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence.” KJV Esther 3:3: “Why transgressest thou the king's commandment?” KJV Esther 3:4: “when they spake daily unto him, and he hearkened not unto them, that they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai's matters would stand: for he had told them that he was a Jew” KJV Esther 3:5: “when Haman saw that Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence, then was Haman full of wrath” KJV Esther 3:6: “wherefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus” Bowing to men elsewhere in the KJV: Genesis 23:7 “And Abraham stood up, and bowed himself to the people of the land”; 1 Samuel 24:8 “David stooped with his face to the earth, and bowed himself” Hebrew (WLC) 3:2: וּמָ֨רְדֳּכַ֔י לֹ֥א יִכְרַ֖ע וְלֹ֥א יִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֶֽה [but Mordecai would not kneel and would not bow down]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 3:2: ὁ δὲ Μαρδοχαῖος οὐ προσεκύνει αὐτῷ. [but Mardochaeus did not do him obeisance]. In a prayer of Mardochaeus that the KJV does not have, the verses labelled 4:17d and 4:17e give a reason: ὅτι οὐκ ἐν ὕβρει, οὐδὲ ἐν ὑπερηφανείᾳ, οὐδὲ ἐν φιλοδοξίᾳ ἐποίησα τοῦτο, τὸ μὴ προσκυνεῖν τὸν ὑπερήφανον Ἀμάν. [that not in insolence, nor in pride, nor in love of glory did I do this, not to do obeisance to the proud Aman] Ἀλλʼ ἐποίησα τοῦτο, ἵνα μὴ θῶ δόξαν ἀνθρώπου ὑπεράνω δόξης Θεοῦ [but I did this that I might not set the glory of a man above the glory of God]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/3/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG03.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG04.htm.
reasoning: Everything that follows in the book turns on this refusal, yet the KJV reports the question put to Mordecai and not his reply. The one clue, that he had told them he was a Jew, is given as the reason the servants informed Haman; it is not said to be the reason he would not bow. In the two other verses quoted, Abraham and David bow to men and the verses record no blame.
scope: Readings, none stated in the KJV verses quoted: that he held bowing to Haman to be forbidden to a Jew; that the refusal was aimed at Haman in particular, for his descent or his person; or that it was a matter between the two men which the book does not tell. The Greek’s added prayer states one reason, that he would not set a man’s glory above God’s; the KJV and the Hebrew edition have no such passage. Genesis 23:7 and 1 Samuel 24:8 were chosen as examples of bowing to men; other passages on bowing were not collected, and the kind of bowing Haman was to receive is not described. This is not presented as a contradiction or as a fault in the passage. title: “Enlargement and deliverance … from another place” — from where, and why would Esther’s house still be destroyed?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Mordecai tells Esther that if she keeps silent, deliverance will come to the Jews “from another place”, but she and her father’s house will be destroyed. He does not say what the other place is, on what he rests his certainty, or by whom her house would be destroyed if the Jews are delivered.
text: KJV Esther 4:13: “Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king's house, more than all the Jews” KJV Esther 4:14: “For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” KJV Esther 4:16: “fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day” Hebrew (WLC) 4:14: רֶ֣וַח וְהַצָּלָ֞ה יַעֲמֹ֤וד לַיְּהוּדִים֙ מִמָּקֹ֣ום אַחֵ֔ר וְאַ֥תְּ וּבֵית־אָבִ֖יךְ תֹּאבֵ֑דוּ [relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place, and thou and thy father’s house will perish]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 4:14: ἄλλοθεν βοήθεια καὶ σκέπη ἔσται τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις· σὺ δὲ καὶ ὁ οἶκος τοῦ πατρός σου ἀπολεῖσθε [from elsewhere help and shelter will be for the Jews; but thou and thy father’s house will perish]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/4/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG04.htm.
reasoning: The sentence is the turning point of Esther’s decision, and it rests on an assurance whose ground is not given. If “another place” means God, the verse does not say so; if it means some other human helper, none is named. The second half is as open: the verse does not say whether Esther’s house would fall in the general slaughter, which the first half says will be averted, or by a judgment on her silence.
scope: Readings, none stated in the verses quoted: that “another place” is a guarded way of speaking of God; that it means another person or power at court; or that Mordecai speaks from confidence in earlier promises to his people, which he does not cite. The Hebrew and the Greek are as general as the KJV here. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV of Esther finds neither “God” nor “Lord” in the book; the Greek names the Lord at 4:8, in words the KJV does not have, and that difference is set out in another record. The fast of 4:16 names no one to whom it is addressed. This is not presented as a contradiction or as a fault in the passage.
